newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE - Shell plumbs natural gas wealth in Peru jungle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Shell plumbs natural gas wealth in Peru jungle.

text.p: Fair-skinned explorers from the Old World descend from still skies into Peru's steamy "New World" jungle, as Indians in flowing brown tunics scurry for cover, unsure what to make of the visit.

With day-glo ball caps, sunburnt faces, and arms tender from a dozen vaccination jabs, Royal Dutch/Shell executives helicopter in to open a health centre for the Cashiriari tribe in Nuevo Mundo, New World in Spanish.

The centre is a donation to thank the community for allowing the oil giant on to its gas-rich land, where Shell has gingerly taken its first steps toward exploiting the Camisea fields, believed to hold six times the rest of Peru's reserves.

A year after the government signed a historic hydrocarbon contract with the Anglo-Dutch firm, Shell, half way through an exploration license, faces close scrutiny from those concerned by its environmental record and alleged indifference to human rights.

If Shell and its non-operating partner Mobil go ahead with drilling in Camisea, Peru would gain $6 billion in tax revenue, wipe out its $400 million annual hydrocarbon trade deficit and become a net exporter.

For 40 years, Shell would draw on the world class reserves, which hold 11 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and 600 million barrels of natural gas liquids, sell the energy to an undersupplied local market and have plenty left to export.
SHELL PLAN UNDER ENVIRONMENTALIST SPOTLIGHT

But with Camisea's natives tracing their culture back 5,000 years, Shell's $3 billion investment plan is in the spotlight as a key test of how its high-tech, profit-seeking business can live alongside indigenous peoples.

Activist groups and company shareholders alike have a sharp eye on Peru's largest foreign investment project seeing that Shell has faced a barrage of criticism in the last couple of years for alleged environmental abuses.

Ahead of a shareholders' vote on a resolution for an independent environmental audit of Shell's activities, a U.S.-based group, Rainforest Action Network, recently presented a stinging report that the firm contaminated Peru's rivers and ignored locals' views.

Still smarting from highly-publicized spats with pressure groups over pollution in Nigeria and plans, since abandoned, to dispose of an oil loading buoy in the north Atlantic, Shell says it limits the environmental impact of its massive Peru operation.
Hovercraft, helicopters and health cards are Shell's basic tools, employed to protect the Cashiriari from overexposure to the modern world.

The tribe is unused to seeing even bicycles in their isolated villages, but the sight of a state-of-the art hovercraft gliding down the mud-brown Urubamba river is now common in the eastern jungle zone, 300 miles (500 km) east of Lima.

The first commercial use of hovercraft in Peru and huge, cargo helicopters have allowed Shell to transport 10,000 tonnes of equipment 45 miles (70 km) from the supply base to its well without eating up the forest with damaging highways.
The oil giant built an airstrip and supply base, and started drilling its appraisal well, but officials claim disturbances to the natives are kept to a minimum.

"We treat it like an offshore operation in the North Sea. There are no roads, everything is flown in and there are explicit orders that only community liaison officers are allowed off-site," Shell Prospecting and Development (Peru) B.V. spokesman Andrew Vickers told Reuters.
VISITORS NEED A HEALTH PASS

Before flying to base camp at Nuevo Mundo, visitors must present a Shell-issued health pass proving the outsider will not infect locals with flu or measles and protecting against the likes of typhoid, hepatitis or yellow fever.

The three-hectare (7.5-acre)appraisal rig site, tucked between the densely-covered Cashiriari hills, is barely noticeable from the air and Shell is already working to replant a third of the land it dug up to drop the well in February.
Confident it has respected Peru's people and its environment, Shell invited President Alberto Fujimori to inspect its groundbreaking project.

But as Fujimori toured the well-site and nearby villages, the stern-faced president gave no clues as to whether he approved of the company's treatment of the locals who eke out a subsistence living along the Urubamba.
"Is he always this stand-offish?" mumbled one oil executive, worried the company had made the wrong impression on the man they wanted to grant them special tax exemptions.

In Cashiriari, Fujimori donned a traditional, brown tunic and feathered headband, doled out clothes and schoolbooks and told the locals -- in front of nodding Shell officials -- they deserved solar-powered electricity at the new health centres.
He also provided Shell's top brass with an example of how to help the locals -- insisting a three-year old boy be airlifted to Lima for immediate surgery on his hairlip.
Aware that a sensitive public has complained bitterly about oil sector privatizations, Shell realises the importance of keeping Fujimori and his Camisea electorate happy.
The multinational has an open-door policy of working with a group of 35 non-governmental organizations that monitors all its operations' impact on the region.
On the group's advice, Shell refused to be lured into granting the tribe's requests for satellite television dishes and instead focuses on "the desperate need for health and education," Vickers said.
And, according to one community leader satisfied by relations with his modern neighbours, the oil giant has done its homework well.
"We are coordinating everything with them and we are not having any problems. Everything is great," beamed Tecori Rios, head of 200 villagers.

Shell also has reason to smile after the government earlier this year awarded it another concession that slots between the two areas -- Blocks 88A and 88B -- of Camisea, creating the possibility of a "golden alley" of natural gas reserves.
Once it has collected data from three appraisal wells in Camisea this year, Shell -- again partnered by Mobil -- plans to invest $22 million exploring the new block.
Shell hopes to produce gas from the Camisea reserves by 1999 and bring the energy to Lima in 2002, but a decision to go ahead with this full development project is still a year away.

But in a sign it believes it can steer through the minefield of criticism, keep the Cashiriari tribe happy and put a smile on Fujimori's face, Shell has already lined up its first clients eager to sign supply contracts by year end.
